clue.text: Student-teacher study-group

parts.note: the whole clue describes a small class where a tutor meets students to study together

explanation.definitionFit: A small teaching session in which a tutor guides one student or a handful is the classic university study meeting.

clue.text: Flower girl with leading TV part

indicators.note: the TV part goes in front, ahead of the girl's name

parts.note: the cathode-ray tube was the main part of an old television set
Rose is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A flower girl appearing on television in the starring role.
explanation.definitionFit: A fragrant white-flowered plant grown from a tuber, prized by perfumers.

clue.text: Carlisle or Southampton in naval terms ?

definitions.text: Carlisle or Southampton in naval terms ?

parts.words: Carlisle or Southampton in naval terms ?
parts.note: towns read as names of Royal Navy vessels: HMS Carlisle and HMS Southampton

explanation.definitionFit: Carlisle and Southampton are English towns whose names were borne by warships, so in navy terms they are town-named vessels; the word also means an administrative district.

clue.text: The end of Pompeii? Remains to be seen

explanation.definitionFit: Destruction was the city's fate under Vesuvius, and the remains of old buildings are what tourists visit there.

clue.text: Mother embraced by chi-chi visitor to the islands ?

annotationWithheld.why: Mother embraced by chi-chi visitor to the islands ? (7): MA can sit inside ANDAMAN, but no reading of 'chi-chi visitor' supplies ANDAN or the rest; no blog or reprint found
annotationWithheld.clue: Mother embraced by chi-chi visitor to the islands ?

clue.text: Backwardness in wartime building

annotationWithheld.why: Backwardness in wartime building (6): the only parse splits 'Backwardness' into indicator 'Backward' and fodder 'ness' (rev of NESS IN = NISSEN), one clue word doing two jobs, which the check refuses

clue.text: Aim, of the Munster Fusiliers? Absurd statement

explanation.definitionFit: A regiment from Munster in Ireland would aim at a bull's-eye; and a self-contradictory statement is traditionally named after the Irish.

clue.text: "O Caledonia ! and wild " (Scott)

parts.note: Scott's Lay of the Last Minstrel has a word missing before 'and wild', which the solver supplies

explanation.walkthrough: Caledonia is the old Latin name for Scotland; the dash in the printed clue is the gap in Scott's line.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott called Scotland harsh and severe, the adjective meaning grim and unbending.

clue.text: Tugmen use this form of flavouring

indicators.note: a new form of the word is made by reshaping its letters

explanation.surface: Tug crews flavour their food with a particular spice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form of' reads as 'kind of flavouring', but 'form' tells you to rearrange TUGMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard seed of a tropical tree is grated as a spice in cooking.

clue.text: Points to a chemist from the marshes

parts.note: S and W are two compass points, south and west
MPS stands for Member of the Pharmaceutical Society, a qualified chemist

explanation.surface: Directions to a pharmacy given by someone who has come in from the wetlands.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a chemist is a pharmacist; MPS (Member of the Pharmaceutical Society) is the old qualification.
explanation.definitionFit: Boggy wetlands are also called bogs or fens.

clue.text: Burlington Bertie's outlook ?

parts.note: Burlington Bertie is the music-hall toff 'from Bow', so his view out would be through something from Bow; the phrase is also slang for a paunch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Burlington Bertie from Bow' is a famous British music-hall song about a penniless would-be gentleman; Bow is a district of East London.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved projecting bay of glass gives an outlook, and the music-hall song places Bertie in Bow, the East London district.

clue.text: Inactive nitre compound ?

indicators.note: a chemical compound mixes its elements, so the letters of the clue's chemical are mixed up

explanation.surface: Nitre, saltpetre, described as a chemical compound that does not react.
explanation.walkthrough: 'compound' looks like a chemistry noun next to nitre but tells you to rearrange NITRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemically unreactive substance, like the noble gases, is described as lifeless or motionless in this sense.

clue.text: Supports tea-breaks for example

explanation.surface: Someone backing the custom of tea-breaks.
explanation.definitionFit: Props that hold things up (a cue's or arm's) are one sense; short pauses from work such as a tea-break are the other.

clue.text: Ma's opportunity to be absolutely quiet ?

parts.note: Ma is an informal word for mother, as is mum
an opportunity is a chance

explanation.surface: Mother finally gets her chance of some peace and silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ma's' reads as a possessive, but supplies MUM; MUM also means silent, which is why the old word means tongue-tied.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adjective for someone silent and tongue-tied, staying completely mute.

clue.text: Jolly saintly great-uncle of the saga

definitions.text: Jolly saintly great-uncle of the saga

parts.words: Jolly saintly great-uncle of the saga
parts.note: in Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga, Jolly Forsyte's great-uncle shares his name with the saint of the July rain-day legend

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an adjective but is a character's name. St Swithin's Day (15 July) is the British weather legend: rain on it means forty more days of rain.
explanation.definitionFit: Jolly is young Jolyon's son, and old Jolyon's twin brother, his great-uncle, bears the name of the English saint whose day is 15 July.

clue.text: Frowns making daily appearance ?

explanation.definitionFit: Frowns are lines on the forehead; a newspaper's top-of-story titles appear every day.

clue.text: Materials for gorges

explanation.definitionFit: Fabrics and substances are one sense; eats greedily, crams oneself, is the verb sense.

clue.text: Tonight's bright features

parts.note: on Guy Fawkes Night, 5 November, the sky is lit by rockets and Catherine wheels

explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle presumably ran around 5 November, Bonfire Night in Britain, when explosive displays are set off.
explanation.definitionFit: Pyrotechnic displays light up the night sky on celebration evenings.

clue.text: She cares for combs !

indicators.note: the words 'She cares' stand for, that is turn into, another word made of the same letters

explanation.surface: A woman who takes good care of her combs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'combs' looks like a noun for hair, but it is a verb: to comb an area is to look through it thoroughly.
explanation.definitionFit: To comb a place is to go through it hunting for something, to scour it.

clue.text: "There is a willow grows a brook " (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "There is a willow grows a brook " (Hamlet)

parts.words: "There is a willow grows a brook " (Hamlet)
parts.note: Gertrude's speech on Ophelia's drowning has a word missing from the line, which the solver supplies

explanation.walkthrough: The dash in the printed clue is the gap in Shakespeare's line, which the answer fills.
explanation.definitionFit: In Gertrude's line the willow leans at an angle over the stream, the word meaning slantwise.

clue.text: The endless tears caused by an insect pest

indicators.note: the word 'The' loses its final letter, its end

parts.note: tears (rhyming with 'bears') are rips

explanation.surface: Tears shed over the damage done by a crop-eating insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' cuts THE to TH. 'tears' reads as crying but means rents.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny winged insects that damage crops and garden plants by sucking sap.

clue.text: What's so hot about the diet ?

definitions.text: What's so hot about the diet ?

parts.words: What's so hot about the diet ?
parts.note: reads as a sceptical question about a fashionable diet, but asks for the unit of heat that dieters count

explanation.definitionFit: It is a unit of heat energy, and slimmers count them in their food.

clue.text: Fellow hired to make a wreath ?

parts.note: a chap is a fellow
to let is to hire out, so let means hired out

explanation.surface: A man hired to make a wreath for a funeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A garland or circlet of flowers worn on the head.

clue.text: Start the race but drop out

explanation.surface: A runner sets off and then quits.
explanation.definitionFit: To shout the start signal for a race is one reading; to withdraw from a commitment is the idiom.

clue.text: Product of the length and breadth of the country?

definitions.text: Product of the length and breadth of the country?

parts.words: Product of the length and breadth of the country?
parts.note: length multiplied by breadth gives a measure of surface, and 'the country' means the countryside rather than the nation

explanation.definitionFit: Multiplying length by breadth gives a surface measure, and a stretch of countryside is called that.

clue.text: It's the sovereign rule !

indicators.note: read as 'it has': the words that follow hold, inside them, the letters of the answer

explanation.surface: A ringing declaration that monarchy is the governing principle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' stands for 'it has': 'the sovereign' has the run of letters inside it, and 'rule' is the definition, not part of the statement.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's period on the throne is the time of royal government.

clue.text: Shrink from the bully

explanation.surface: Recoiling in fear from a tormentor.
explanation.definitionFit: To cringe in fear is one sense; one who intimidates (cows) others is the other, a cow-er.

clue.text: Wide valley on Dartmoor

parts.note: the West Country word for a hollow or valley, found in many Devon place-names

explanation.walkthrough: Dartmoor is a national park in Devon, south-west England, where this word for a valley is common in place-names.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect word for a hollow or valley in south-west England; Dartmoor is a moorland in Devon.

clue.text: He provides a belt of overhead lighting

definitions.text: He provides a belt of overhead lighting

parts.words: He provides a belt of overhead lighting
parts.note: sounds like an electrician, but the belt is three stars in the night sky worn by a hunter constellation

explanation.definitionFit: The constellation named after the Greek hunter shows a row of three bright stars known as his belt.

clue.text: C-in-C on arctic trek ?

parts.note: the Arctic is the region round the North Pole
a trek is a long march

explanation.surface: A commander-in-chief leading a long journey across the polar ice.
explanation.walkthrough: C-in-C is commander-in-chief; in ancient Greece the title was given to a war-leader.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Athens this officer was the military commander, the war-archon.

clue.text: It's very close for a photo

definitions.text: It's very close for a photo

parts.words: It's very close for a photo
parts.note: a race end so tight that a camera must decide the winner

explanation.definitionFit: A race whose end is too tight to call needs a photo to settle it, and the end of a race is its winning line.

clue.text: No dog-backing types, these

parts.note: the word dog read backwards gives a deity, so people who do not back a deity are unbelievers

explanation.walkthrough: 'dog-backing' sounds like supporting dogs, but 'dog' backwards is GOD.
explanation.definitionFit: Unbelievers who deny any deity exists.
